messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Heller, a 34-year-old White American school counselor, presented for his initial intake appointment approximately fourteen months after the event that he described, with visible effort, as the worst moment of his life. He is married and, by his own account, has spent the better part of the past year trying to ensure that his wife and colleagues never fully understand what he carries.

The incident occurred on a Saturday afternoon in late autumn when Marcus was driving home from a school district professional development conference. He was fatigued and, by his own admission, had been managing a persistent headache all day. On a two-lane rural highway, he drifted partially into the oncoming lane. The driver of the approaching vehicle swerved hard to avoid a head-on collision, lost control, and struck a guardrail. Marcus pulled over immediately. When he reached the other car, he found a man in his fifties slumped against the steering wheel, unresponsive, his face lacerated and his arm bent at an angle that made clear something was badly broken. Marcus called 911 and knelt beside the man, pressing his jacket against the wound on the man's forehead. What he has never been able to fully articulate — what seems to stop his speech entirely when he approaches it — is the smell: engine fluid, blood, and something sharper underneath, something he cannot name and cannot forget. The man survived but sustained a traumatic brain injury and required months of inpatient rehabilitation. Marcus was not charged with any offense. He was told, repeatedly, that it was an accident. He has never believed it.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself replaying the moment of impact — not as a memory he could observe from a distance, but as something immediate and total. When it came, it arrived with the full weight of sensation: the sound of the other car hitting the guardrail, the cold of the pavement under his knees, and above all that smell, which had no clean translation into language but which he recognized instantly whenever something approximated it — a hospital antiseptic, a particular kind of cleaning solvent used in the school's maintenance closet, gasoline at a filling station. Each time, his body responded as though the event were unfolding in the present moment: his heart rate spiked, his hands trembled, and he was briefly unable to locate himself in time.

He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that he was not a person who could be trusted to act correctly when it mattered. This belief had taken on particular weight in his professional life. As a school counselor, Marcus regularly encounters students in distress, and what had once felt like a natural competence now felt like a performance conducted over a void. He had begun keeping his mind relentlessly occupied — reviewing student case notes, listening to podcasts during every commute, filling silences at home with television — because stillness was when the memory arrived uninvited. He avoided thinking about the event directly, and he had developed a careful habit of rerouting his drives to avoid passing the stretch of highway where it happened, which added nearly twenty minutes to his commute each day.

When a routine physical was scheduled last spring, Marcus cancelled it twice. The thought of a medical examination — the clinical smell of the room, the procedural handling of his body — produced a dread he could not explain to his wife without telling her more than he was prepared to say. He had also stopped taking a shortcut near the local police precinct, uncertain of what he felt when he saw a patrol car but knowing that whatever it was, it was not manageable in public.

His wife had noticed the distance. She had named it, gently and then less gently, over several months. It was ultimately her quiet statement — that she felt she was living with someone who had decided to disappear — that brought Marcus to the referral. He arrived at intake exhausted, guarded, and carrying the particular shame of a man who helps others process difficulty for a living and has been unable to apply any of that to himself. What he feared most was confirming what he already suspected: that the accident had not merely changed him, but had revealed something about him that had always been true.
